descriptions.Keres: First let's have a look at the position. Well, it is quite a position! Who is actually better off? Difficult. [+2.8] Let's have a look at what can be taken; are there any immediate attacks? 1. Bh6 [+0.3] and 2. Nxf7 - not sufficient [two moves in a row]. 1. Nxc6 maybe? [+0.3] He must take back with the pawn; with the rook costs a pawn and with the queen will not be possible either - indeed - so 1. Nxc6 1... bxc6, 2. Bxd5 2... cxd5, 3.qf3. Pfui! That seems to win a piece. (Pause) The pawn at b2 is attacked. Right off 1. Bxd5 maybe? [correct move] Nothing special. Let's calculate it though: 1... Bxd5 [engine slightly prefers exd5], 2. Bxf6 [implied Bxf6] and 3. Nd7 - possibly even 3. Nxd5 first [both good]. 1... Nxd5 costs a piece. 1... exd5, 2. Qf3 maybe? let's check 2. Qf3. What should black do? 2... Kg7, then for instance, 3. Ng4 - will probably win. Well, white will win after 1. Bxd5
descriptions.Alekhine: At first sight there is a dark memory of a tournament game Botvinnik-Vidmar (Nottingham). There's a certain resemblance: the same queen position on d3. Opening type: queen's gambit accepted. In half an hour I should be able to logically reconstruct the moves up to this position. Is the pawn at b2 really attacked? Or isn't that essential? See what counter possibilities white has. Which moves are worth considering? 1. Bxd5 - to calculate: 1... Bxd5 is no good, 1... Nxd5 is no good, so 1... exd5. And then the knight at f6 is getting a little weak. 2. Ng4 [+0.3] or 2. Rfe1 [or Rce1, ambiguous] might follow or also 2. Nxc6 [+0.5] and 3. Rfe1 [ambiguous again], or possibly 2. Qf3. Well, in any case 1. Bxd5 is the one enticing move. But now let's have a look at other possibilities: 1. Ng4 deserves consideration, but doesn't look so good [-3.6]. 1. Nxd5 maybe, 1... Nxd5, 2. Bxd5, 2... Bxg5 [-1.3] with many capturing possibilities but at first sight not convincing. 1. Nxc6. at first sight 1... bxc6 would follow and then d5 gets stronger, that's a pity. In any case white has by far the best of it [+0.2] I would be very happy if I had such a position in a tournament game. Are there any other moves, apart from 1. Bxd5 that are decisive? 1. Bxd5 is very strong, that much is certain. 1. Nxc6 to calculate [again!]: 1... bxc6, pressure on c6, the pair of bishops: also very agreeable, but the position promises more. Check over other sorts of things again. Well, in case of time pressure I would play 1. Bxd5.
descriptions.Flohr: It's been a queen's gambit accepted or Karo-Kann. f6 is weak, but d5 is a strong point; the pawn on d4 is isolated and, as such, weak. White's chances are in the attack, black's in the endgame. 1. Nxd5 or perhaps 1. Bxd5 deserve consideration. 1. Bxd5 looks good. Let's calculate it: does it give a decisive advantage? No other move would win immediately in any case. One must first see if there is anything decisive in the position. 1. Bxd5 and now only 1... exd5 is possible, and then one plays for instance 2. Qf3 or 2. Ref1 [ambiguous again]. No direct decision. Maybe first neutralize the bishop at c6. 1. Nxc6, then 1... bxc6. Then for instance proceed positionally with 2. Na4 [+0.2]. Also possible is 1. Nxc6, 2. Bxd5 and 3. Qf3. 1. Nxc6 is a good move in any case, if there is nothing decisive, then one should hold on to a small advantage. The pair of bishops and the weak pawns for black. But wait, can't you win the exchange? Yes: 1. Nxc6, 1... bxc6 - forced, 1... Rxc6 doesn't hold - 2.Bxd5, 2... cxd5, 3. Bxf6 and 4. Nd7 (sic) [??]. Yes, 1. Nxc6 looks good, I play that. [incorrect]
descriptions.Fine: It has been a Caro-Kann or a queen's gambit accepted. Obviously black has to defend himself against an attack along the diagonal with g6. White has to play for the attack, otherwise he has nothing. Must he go for f7? Or not? Black has few threats. Qxg6 is probably impossible. Or is it? Let's try. 1. Ng4 - take it away. 1. Qd2 [-3.5] - then black exchanges on my c3 and plays 2... Ne4, so that won't work [correct reasoning]. 1. Nxd5 - not satisfactory. 1. Ref1 [no ambiguity!] for instance: 1... Qxb2, 2. Bxd5, 2... Nxd5, 3. Bxe7, 3... Nxe7, 4. Rb1, 4... Qxa3, 5. Nd5, 5... Qxd3 - there's nothing there [full of mistakes, but correct conclusion]. Maybe another way: 1. Rfe1, 1... Qxb2, 2. Bxd5, 2...Nxd5 - 2... Bxd5 is no good - 3. Nxd5, 3... Bxg5, 4. Rb1, 4... Qa2 - or 4... Qd7? No, then 5. Ne7+ - and then Qxd2. White has nothing. 1. Rfe1, 1... Qxb2 and now something else: also unsatisfactory. (Short pause) But what about 1. Bxd5? If 1... Bxd5, the exchange is lost, if 1... Nxd5, he loses a piece, so black must play 1... exd5. Then maybe 2. Rfe1 or even better 2. Qf3 or 2. Ng4. Yes, 1. Bxd5 is the best move.
descriptions.Euwe: First impression: an isolated pawn, white has more freedom of movement. Black threatens Qxb2. Is it worthwhile to parry that? It probably is; if he takes, then a3 is also attacked. Can white then take advantage of the open file? Does not look like it. Still again: 2. Nxc6 [unclear which position] and then by exchange the pawn at a3 is defended by the queen. Indirectly in connection with the hanging position of the knight at f6 and possibly because of the overburdening of the bishop at e7. But wait a moment: no, Qxb2 is rather unpleasant after all because the bishop at a2 is undefended. Can I do something myself? Investigate that first: the pieces on f6 and d5 are both somewhat tied down. Let us look at the consequences of some specific moves. 1. Nxd5, possibly preceded by 1. Nxc6. Then 1... Rxc6 is probably impossible because of taking on d5. Black has a number of forced moves, there may be a possibility to take advantage of that. It is not yet quite clear. Let us look at other attacks: 1. Bh6 in connection with f7 - but I don't really see how to get at it. 1. b4 [-0.3] in order to parry the threat - but then exchange on c3 will give some difficulties in connection with 2... Bb5 - oh no, that is not correct, one can take back with the queen. So far a somewhat disorderly preliminary investigation. Now, let's look in some more detail at the possibilities for exchange: 1. Nxc6 or 1. Nxd5, or maybe 1. Bxd5, or maybe first 1. Bxf6. 1. Nxc6, 1... Rxc6; 2. take on d5, for instance 2. Nxd5, 2... exd5, wins a pawn, but there may be compensation for black on b2. But better is 2... Nxd5 [correct], then 3. Bxd5, 3... Rxc1 is nearly forced, no, it is not, he can play 3... Bxg5 as well [both about equal]. I see no immediate advantage. 1... exd5 is not forced therefore; and even if it were forced you couldn't be quite sure of winning. It's happened before that such a position proved less favorable than it seemed to be. The point d5 is reinforced by it, that is a disadvantage. 1. taking on d5. 1. Nxc6 at any rate gives the pair of bishops; if I don't find anything better, I can always do this. 1. Nxd5, 1... Bxd5; is that possible? [+1.3] d7 is free then. 2. Bxf6, 2... Bxf6, 3. Nd7, 3... Qd8 can then be done. [+4, ??] 1. Nxd5, 1... Bxd5, 2. Bxf6, 2... Bxf6 will probably yield something. 1... Nxd5 is also possible; maybe better. Then 2. Bxd5, 2... Bxg5 and now there are possibilities to take on c6, or to play something like b4; once again: 1. Nxd5, 1... Nxd5, 2. Bxf6, 2... Bxf6 - no, nothing then, 3. Rxc6 does not help any; it is a cute move but at the end of it all everything remains hanging. Something else: 2. Bxe7 - he just takes back. 1... exd5 is very favorable; he won't do that, it needn't be investigated. 1. Nxd5, 1... Nxd5 remains. 2. Bxd5, 2... Bxg5, 3. Bxc6, 3... Bxc1 is then possible. No, can find no way to make anything out of this. 1... Nxd5, 2. Bh6, 2... Rfd8, 3. Qf3 [-0.4] with some threats; if black now has to play his bishop back to e8, then one gets a good position [correct, +0.6]. 1. Bxd5: this must be looked into. Does that make any difference? 1. Bxd5, 1... Bxd5 is again impossible because of 2. Nd7 [+0.1]. That is to say, we will have to look out for 2... Bc4, but that we can probably cope with: the worst that can happen to me is that he regains the exchange, but then I have in any case some gain of time. 1. Bxd5, 1... Nxd5; 2. same difficulties as just before. No, that is now impossible: 2. Nxd5 now wins a piece. 1. Bxd5, 1... Bxd5, 2. Bxf6, 2... Bxf6, 3. Nd7, 3... Qd8. Let's have a closer look at that: 4. Nxd5, 4... exd5 and I'm an exchange to the good: very strong. 1. Bxd5, 1... exd5 is therefore forced. But that's good for white. The knight on f6 is weak, the bishop at e7 [possible mistake - says K6??] hangs - and the bishop on c6 stands badly. On positional grounds one could already decide on 1. Bxd5. Is there some immediate gain? 1. Bxd5, 1... exd5; it looks bad for black. Probably some more accidents will soon happen. Much is still up in the air. One plays, for instance, 2. Qf3. Defending the knight on f6 is not so easy; 2... Kg7 looks very unpleasant. Yes, I play 1. Bxd5.
descriptions.Prins: The first thing that strikes me is the weakness of the black king's wing, particularly the weakness at f6. Only after that a general picture of the position. Finally, the complications in the center are rather striking: possibilities for exchange in connection with the loose bishop on e7. Still later: my pawn on b2 is en prise. Now work out the complications: 1. Ng4 perhaps? Rather 1. Bxd5, or perchance 1. Bh6 in order to weaken f7. Let's work through the possibilities in the position; the counterchances of black? If the bishop on g5 goes away, for example, in case of Bxf8 [when B was on h6], then ... Nf4 and my g2 is attacked: I don't feel quite safe. Now let's calculate 1. Bxd5; that is after all the most plausible: 1. Bxd5; if black now retakes with the bishop or with the pawn, then 2. Ng4, and if black takes, then 3. Bxe7 and white is better off. Go over 1. Bxd5 again... Is there a calm move to prepare the attack? Maybe 1. Qh3 with the threat of 2. Qh4. It looks very strong. But now a drawback appears: on 1. Qh3, Qxd4 follows. So it doesn't hold up. 1. Bxd5 again. 1... Bxd5, 2. Ng4, then the zwischenzug 2... Bc4! Complicated, difficult to calculate. Perhaps another move is better after all? 1. b4 with the threat of driving the bishop away and then taking on d5? No, then he plays 1... Nxc3 and if then 2. Rxb3, then 2... Bb5. Rather disagreeable. 1. Bxd5 again; 1... Bxd5, 2. Ng4, 2... Bc4. Is that really serious? Wait a minute: white can play 3. Bxf6 with a mate threat. So that's refuted. Now to look over everything again. It's becoming clearer. 1. Bxd5 is the move. (Afterthoughts: 1. Ng4 'feeling': personal preference: knight to the king's wing, besides it takes advantage of the weakness on f6 and of the hanging position of the bishop on e7. (Results in nothing; from there probably to) Take on d5? (the intention is to win the bishop on e7 or some such thing. That doesn't succeed after 1. Nxd5, 1... Nxd5, 2. Bxd5, 2... Bxg5! Therefore): postpone Nxd5 (with the gain of tempo) until the second move, thus 1. Bxd5. Now begin with the probably bad countermoves - in order to be able to eliminate those - so 1. Bxd5, 1... Nxd5? then 2. Nxd5, etc. 1... exd5 looks bad; white not only has 2. Ng4 then but also 2. Qf3 at his command. (1. Bxd5), 1... Bxd5; 2. Ng4 would be very strong. White stands better; temporarily let it be. A stupid move perhaps? 1. Bh6; if that should prove even stronger, then I don't have to figure out all the variants of 1. Bxd5. Or 1. b4 to 'quietly' strengthen the attack? After an easygoing move, must take into account the counterchances of black, notably along the diagonal from my f1 to b5, or on f4 if the white bishop disappears. Now a better calculation of 1. Bxd5, 1... Bxd5, 2. Ng4. Now further: 2... Kg7, 3. Bh6+ [+4], etc. 2... Qd8 cannot be good [correct] because after Nxd5 and Rxc8 the queen must retake on c8: such as 3. Bxf6, 4. Nxd5, and 5. Rxf8 winning a piece on f6. 2... Nxg4, 3. Bxe7, 3... Rfe8, 4. Bg5 [Qg3 is better here, Bg5 gives -1.1] and white has the pair of bishops, at least one very good bishop. His knight on g4 is in trouble; weakened position. Calm move? 1. Qh3, Qh4? In order to make use of f6 and h6? No, the pawn on d4. Then something else will go wrong. Once again. 1. Bxd5, 1... Bxd5, 2. Ng4 (now black has a choice) 2... Bc4! Troubles. Temporarily dismiss that. 1. b4 threatens b5; then the bishop must go to e8 - Bd7 can't be good - that's not attractive for black. So 1. b4 - no, then comes 1... Nxc3 and the rook cannot retake on account of 2... Bb5. Well, it can for that matter, but it's not nice: the advantage is gone. Then here we go again with 1. Bxd5. On 1... exd5, 2. Qf3 possibly followed by Ng4 which cannot be good for black. 1... Bxd5, 2. Ng4. Oh yes, now 2... Bc4. Is there nothing then? Ignore it? Yes, 3. Bxf6 threatens Nh6 mate - then on 3... Bxd3 follows 4. Nh6 mate. But in case of 2... Bc4, 3. Bxf6, 3... Bxf6? Well, then something like 4. Qf3, [-2.6] 4... Bxf1 [+2.1], 5. Nxf6+ and 6. Rxf1; that wins. Well, 3. Bxf6 is good. Now just a short recapitulation: 1. Bxd5. Not 1... Nxd5 now, and in case of 1... exd5, 2. Qf3 and white stands splendidly. So 1. Bxd5, 1... Bxd5. Then... look over everything quickly. Quite satisfies me. So: 1. Bxd5.
descriptions.Cortlever: count pawns, pieces. White's position is good, but for the endgame not so good. Will probably have to try and attack on the king. 1. Bxf6 and then 2. Nxd5 - to eliminate my weak pawn maybe; if 1... Bxf6, 2.Nxd5 then 2... exd5 and the weakness is already gone; and on 1... Nxf6 maybe 2. d5? 1. Bh6 maybe; not so very promising. 1. Nxd5, taking immediately on d5? An annoying sort of position! With such a rotten pawn (d4)! Now let us calculate some: 1. Bxf6, 1... Bxf6, 2. Nxd5, 2... exd5, 3. Ng4, 3... Bxd4 - not so good. 1. h4 is possible too [+1]; taking on f6, h4, h5 and Bb1, etc. to attack. Does black threaten anything? Not much to speak of. 1. Nxd5, then comes 1... Nxd5. 1. Bxf6 again; 1... Nxf6, 2. d5, takes; 3. takes and then Rd1 [ambiguous] - bad. Let us look around for other possibilities. 1. h4 followed by Bb1. 1. Ng4 immediately maybe, or: 1. B4. Then 1... Nxc3, 2. Rxc3, Bd5, and now 3. Bxf6 and 4. Bxd5? Nothing, that's a draw. Just look at the position. 1. Bb1 [-0.4] maybe? Can he then take the pawn on b2? Yes, so 1. b4 perchance? Don't like it. 1. Nxd5 - calculate that somewhat better now: 1. Nxd5, 1... Nxd5, 2. Bxd5, 2... Bxg5, 3. Bxc6, 3... Bxc1, 4. Rxc1, 4... Qxb2 [+1.8] 5. Rb1 - something like that? Other variants of this: 1. Nxd5, 1... Nxd5, 2. Bxd5, 2... Bxg5, 3. Bxc6, 3... Bxg5, 4. f4, 4... Bxd5, 5. fxg5 [-8.7]. No result. Something else to that move? 1. Nxd5, 1... Nxd5, 2. Bxd5, 2... Bxg5, 3. Bxc6, 3... Bxc1, 4. Rxc1, 4... bxc6, 5. Nd7, 5... Qxb2, 6. Rb1, 6... Qa2, 7. Nxf8 [-1.2, some good alternatives missed]. The alternative: 1. Nxd5, 1... Nxd5, 2. Bxd5, 2... Bxg5, 3. Bxc6, 3... Bxc1, 4. Rxc1, 4... Rxc6, 5. Nxc6, 5... bxc6 - somewhat better [0.0]. Once more: 1. Nxd5, 1... Nxd5, 2. Bxd5, 2... Bxg5, 3. Bxc6, 3... Bxc1. How is the material situation now? Three pieces against bishop and rook ... and knight - so an exchange down. But then maybe immediately 4. Nd7; no, then 4... Qxc6 follows, so it is better to take back on c1. 1. Nxd5, 1... Nxd5, 2. Bxd5, 2... Bxg5, 3. Bxc6, 3... Bxc1, 4. Rxc1, 4... bxc6, 5. Nd7, 5... Qd8, 6. Nxf8 works well. But black can play differently: 5... Qxb2; now maybe 6. Qe3, 6... Rfd1, 7. Nf6+, 7... Kg7, 8. Ng4 [-5.6] - that hardly can be correct: too crazy. Now again a general inspection; other moves. 1. Ne4: also a good move. 1. Rfe1 the same. The knight on c3 cannot move very well on account of Bb5. But: 1. Nxc6 does not appeal to me. 1. Nxd5, 1... Nxd5, 2. Bxd5, 2... Bxg5, 3. f4, 3... exd5 - does not appeal to me very much either. Perhaps common moves are better: 1. Qg3 to h4 is weak. 1. Rfd1 to prepare it, 1... Qxb2. Then 2. Nc4, I win the queen! Is there perhaps some counterchance for black? No, indeed the queen is caught. 1. Rfd1 for Qg3 and also against Bb5. If now 1... Nxc3 then 2. bxc3. Better for white. 1. Rfd1, 1... Rfd8; then still follow the same recipe. 2. Qh3 - stronger than 2. Qg3 - and possibly a sacrifice on f7. Then rather 1. Rfe1 - pleasant on the open e file; 1... Rfd8 for instance; 2. Qh3, threatens Nxf7. The other rook can then defend d4; it isn't doing much on the c file anyhow. 1... Qxb2 still doesn't work because of 2. Nc4. Pressure on f7, e6. Pleasant. 1. Rfe1 is my move. [missed 1... Nxc3, only +0.4]
descriptions.Landau: Let's have a look. White's position is superior in any case. To search for a combination in connection with f6 and d5. To figure out 1. Bxd5, with possibly Nd7 afterwards, in case black takes back with the bishop. 1... Bxd5 then later Nd7; so 1... exd5 is forced; but one doesn't get very far with that either. Let's look at 1. Nxc6. Also important. Calculate 2. Nxd5, to see if that provides any direct advantage. 1. Nxc6, 1... Rxc6, 2. Nxd5, 2... Nxd5, 3. Bxd5, 3... Rxc1 probably leads to nothing [0.0]. 4. Rxc1, 4... Bxg5 [-5.5]; but wait a moment, also 4. Bxc1 is possible [0.0]. What then? Let's have another look: 1. Nxc6, 1... Rxc6, 2. Nxd5, 2... Nxd5, 3. Bxd5, 3... Rxc1. Now something else: 4. Bxe7, 4... Rxf1+, 5. Qxf1 [-1.7, Kx is 0.0], 5... Re8, 6. Bc5 probably to the advantage of white [-0.1]. But it can be played otherwise: 5... exd5, 6. Bxf8 - haven't achieved much then [-1.7]; leads indeed to nothing. Look for something else: 1. Nxc6, 1... Rxc6, 2. Nxd5, 2... Nxd5. Now something else? No, doesn't yield much. 1. Nxd5, 1... Nxd5; what then? 2. Bxe7, 2... Nxe7 - nothing. There is no decisive combination. Then maybe an ordinary attacking move: 1. h4 for instance; but what then on 1... Qxb2? Is there any compensation then for the pawn? Probably not [Nc4 was missed]. 1. Bh6 maybe. See if anything comes out of that. (short pause) Still, I keep looking at taking on d5; there might be something in it. 1. Nxd5 or 1.Bxd5. If 1. Bxd5, then 1... Nxd5 is impossible. 1... Bxd5 would be forced, there fore - but that has its drawbacks too: loss of the exchange. Yes, 1. Bxd5 is the move. With that white gets the advantage. 1... exd5 is forced, and then a favorable position is reached. Play 2. f4 for instance. Maybe we can get even more out of it. 1. Bxd5, 1... exd5, 2. Nxd5 in order to win a pawn possibly? No, that doesn't work. Let's look at 2. Qf3. Then 2... Qd8 is forced. What then? 1. Bxd5, 1... exd5. A combination with 2. Bxf6, 2... Bxf6, 3. take on d5 and Nd7 - insufficient. 1. Bxd5 followed by 2. f4 is probably the best. Maybe a better continuation? Yet possible perhaps to get material advantage? Search for something. Once again: 1. Nxd5, 1... Nxd5, 2. Bxe7, 2... Nxe7. Does that yield anything? No, better is 1. Bxd5, 1... exd5; and now? What further? In any case, 1. Nxd5 is good.
descriptions.Weinstein: Well, I see my queen isn't en prise anyway. Ah, yeah, diagonal is closed. 1. Bh6 puts the, ah, rook in an odd position. Let's see. 1. Qh3 - there's a move, but ah, might have some Qh4 possibilities. My b2 is en prise - got to watch the b2 pawn - yeah the b2 pawn is important. However, 1. Bx.... 1. Bxd5, 1... Nxd5, 2. Nxd5, wins a piece. 1. Bxd5, 1... Bxd5, 2. Nxd5. Ah wait a second, wait a second - there's some sort of , ah, some sort of idea there: 1. Bxd5, 1... Bxd5, 2. Nxd5, 2... exd5. I play 1. Bxd5. I don't see it all, but I see that 1. Bxd5... Oh, wait a second, there's another possibility ... hmmmm ... yes, there's still another possibility: 1.Bxd5, 1... exd5; there's a possibility of playing, ah, playing what? 1. Bxd5, 1... exd5. I play 1. Bxd5 mainly because it gets rid of my weakness, and I have some queen move with a tempo. For instance, I can play 2. Qf3; if he plays 2... Qd8, I don't see that I've gained anything definite except his rooks are unconnected now, and I still have the initiative. All right, I play 1.Bxd5.
descriptions.Heemskerk: Both sides have equal material. The knight on e5 is good for white. (Looks silently) 1. b4 because the b2 pawn is attacked; but then my knight on c3 becomes a bit 'weak'. Let's look at 1. Nxd5, 1... Bxd5 is not good - then I take again and 2... exd5 is not then possible because he loses the exchange. Indeed, he loses the exchange. 1... Nxd5, 2. Bxd5, 2... Bxg5; and then what might turn up I don't know. No, 2. Bxd5 is not good because after 2... Bxg5 the rook on c1 is also under attack. Disadvantage. So rather 2. Bxe7, 2... Nxe7. Let's look at 1. Ng4 - that's not very good: ...Qxb2 follows. 1. Nxd5, 1... Nxd5, 2. Bxe7, 2... Nxe7, 3. b4 then probably. White's better off - I'm prejudiced. Yes, my move is 1. Nxd5 [incorrect]
descriptions.Roodzant: First have a look at the material. Count pawns. White has an isolated pawn. Look at how many pieces of white and of black are under attack. The queen at d3 is undefended. Two white pieces are attacked. On the basis of the fact that white attacks more men in the black position, he is better off. Still, to see how many squares one controls. (Many short pauses in between here). The knight on e5 exerts quite a pressure on black's position. Moreover, g7 is weakened; white's king wing has not been weakened. Let's look for how white can best get on the attack. Also examine whether the hanging bishop on e7 can be profited from. First by exchanging moves leaving it undefended and then to profit from that. Doubling the rooks on the c file is also possible; then b4, b5 in order to attack his rook on c8 twice. 1. Nxd5 is what I'm looking at. Can't get any decent advantage. 1... Nxd5, 2. Bxe7, 2... Nxe7; then indeed I've gotten his knight back on e7. But on the other hand, the diagonal of his bishop on c6 is open. No great advantage. Also look at 1. Bh6. Perhaps I would play here: 1. Rc2 and then see about continuing with b4, b5. (E: in a real tournament game would you make your move on the basis of all this?) No, it's very difficult. I'm looking now at combinations in connection with 1. Qh3. Exchange on d5 often enough so that he has to retake with the pawn and then his rook on c8 is once again attacked. Perhaps 1. f4 is playable [-1.9] in order to continue with f5. 1. f4 could indeed be played; then he cannot play 1... h6, for I just take it; the rook gets a free file (f file). Then also the queen comes in with it. In any case white will have to extract some profit from that weakness after all. Yes, methinks that 1. f4 is the best to play, with the intention of chasing the bishop away with f5. If 1... Nxc3, then 2. Rxc3 and Rfc1. But wait, then he can play 2... Bb5, and then I have to exchange my rook at c3 and his rook will get on the open file and ... then I must lose the exchange. But I also can take back with the queen, 2. Qxc3; then after 2... Bb5, 3. Qxc8 gets two rooks for the queen. Doubling rooks is OK then, but then the pawn on d4 gets lost. So on 1... Nxc3, 1. f4 actually runs ashore. 1. Qf3 should be looked at - but that is idiotic to go stand on the bishop's diagonal. The intention was to exchange twice on d5 and then have an attack on f7. Let me look at 1. Ne4, 1... Nxe4, 2. Qxe4 doesn't work, then the bishop on g5 falls - and then, too, the queen stands in the bishop's line. Let's look once if any attacks on the black queen are possible. Can we get her under the fire of light pieces? But what if I just take off the bishop? 1. Nxc6; if bxc6, then a weak pawn; so 1... Rxc6, then 2. Ne4, 2... Nxe4 - or 2... Rxc1, but then my rook gets the open file - and then 3. Bxe7. Let's see if all that's true: 1. Nxc6; Qxc6 is now out of the way: queen stands in the line of the rook; so 1... Rxc6, 2. Ne4, 2... Nxe4, 3. Bxe7. ...Oh, wait a moment, that knight (on d5) is still here; the bishop on e7 is covered. Then another way is 2. Nxd5, 2... Rxc1, then 3. Nxe7+ wins a piece. 2... Nxd5, then 3. Bxd5 and I attack the queen (sic); he must answer that and I win something: the bishop at e7. And if he plays 2... exd5, then a pawn on a white square on the bishop's diagonal is also favorable. Yes, I play 1. Nxc6. [incorrect]
descriptions.De Groot, E1: White has more room. Look further. The pawn at b2 is attacked. Can it be taken? Quite probably; a threat. 1. b4 is to be considered. Does it threaten anything? Hardly. f6 is weak, and white has more room; he is probably somewhat better off. 1. b4 simplifies too much; not so strong. Look for a combination; maybe something there. 1. Nxc6, 1... Rxc6, 2. Bxf6 and 3. d5 maybe. How to make use of the weakness of f6, and then to weaken e6? Thus 3. d5, takes, takes, takes: general exchange, without advantage, rather disadvantage. 1. Nxd5 does not lead to anything either. 1. Bxd5; is that something? To take back with the bishop is impossible; 1... Nxd5 doesn't work either, so 1... exd5 is forced. And then maybe 2. Bxf6, 2... Bxf6, 3. rook takes bishop (sic) and 4. Nd7. But then comes simply 4... Qd8 - no advantage. 1. Bxd5 may still be good. Let's look at 1... exd5, 2. Qf3. No, then comes 2. Qd8. It is a pity to waste the king's bishop if nothing comes of it. Let's again calculate the variant with 3. rook takes bishop. So 1. Bxd5, 1... exd5, 2. Bxf6, 2... Bxf6, 3. rook takes bishop; 4. Nd7, 4... Qd8 [no idea what he's talking about]. Does this lead to anything? Apparently doesn't go any further. 1. Bxd5, 1... exd5, 2. Bxf6, 2... Bxf6, 3. rook takes bishop (sic), 3... pawn takes rook; 4. Nd7, 4... Qd8. Get back the exchange, then probably nothing more: 5. Nx rook [?], 5... king takes knight. What then? Pawn on d5 is covered, pawn on d4 undefended. Is there anything to be done then? 6. Qb5 for example? Then the pawn on d4 hangs - nothing special. Let's look at new variants. These are not clear. White stands better though, so there should be something.  And 1. Bxd5 looks like a strong move - I don't know why I cling so to 1. Bxd5. 1. Bxf6 - I don't believe in that. 1. Bxd5 and 2. Bxf6 I keep coming back to. 1. Bxd5 and 2. Qf3 maybe. There must be something to that. But no, that is no good either. There follows 2... Kg7 or 2... Qd8. The pawn at b2 is attacked. Is that a threat I should be worried about? 1. Bxd5, 2. Bxf6 and 3. h4 perhaps, to assault the king's wing? Or maybe: 1. h4. What to play after 1... Qxb2 - on an indifferent move, 2. h5 follows. But wait! 2. Nc4 costs a queen [black queen trapped]. Yes, so 1. h4 now deserves consideration. What will black play? Probably prevent h5. If 1... Nxc3, then 2. bxc3 again threatening h5. Maybe 2... Rfe8 or something, to cover the bishop on e7. He cannot play 2... Bxa3 because the knight on f6 is hanging. Is there another move for black? Once again 3. h5 is threatened; is this simple to parry? Go on calculating 1. Bxd5 again. 1. Bb1 also comes into consideration. (E: now you're gradually beginning to get into time pressure) Still look quickly at a few things; weigh things. Yes, 1. Bb1 [-0.4] is my move, later to be followed by h4. [incorrect]
descriptions.De Groot, E2: Equal number of pieces. (Again silently looks at the position) 'By feel' white is somewhat better. f6 and such are weak. Is there anything to get at, to pick out an immediate advantage? Take the knight on d5 perhaps? 1. Ne4 maybe, 1... Nxe4, 2. Qxe4 doesn't work so 2. Bxe7, 2... Nxe7 - no. 1. Bh6, rook moves; nothing special. 1. h4 perhaps to get to h5. Every once in a while I feel like playing such a move in such a position. Threatens 2. h5, so maybe his weakening g6 can be exploited. What will black play? Probably 1... Rfd8 to consistently hit away at d4. But then 2. h5 is perhaps already immediately possible [+2.7]. 2... Nxh5 doesn't work, 2... gxh5 looks very bad. So it's probably better not to play 1. Rfd8 but to cover the king bishop or move it away. For example 1... Rfe8; then 2. h5 is prevented. But then white can nicely play 2. Rfe1 in order then to play h5 again, eventually. Then Nxh5 is again impossible because the bishop on e7 hangs. Go over 1. h4 again... Yes, I play 1. h4. [incorrect]
descriptions.De Groot, E3: Have a look at the position. White's better. Have a look. Does the capture on d5 yield anything? 1. Nxd5 followed by Qf3 maybe? 1... Bxd5 doesn't work because of 2. Bxd5 and loss of the exchange. 1. Nxd5, 1... Bxd5 indeed loses the exchange, but can black maybe win it back; by 2... Bb5 (sic) or something like that? Probably not. How does black take back on d5 then? With the pawn thus. 1. Nxd5 - let's calculate all the variants. How to exploit the weakness of f6, perhaps simultaneously with a threat on d5. 1. Nxd5, 1... exd5, 2. Qf3 or something. Pawn on d4 hangs; that makes matters more difficult. Search for possibilities in order to reach something positive. (Calculations) 1. Qh3 maybe, or as a second move (after 1. Nxd5) 2. Qh3. Then the queen has two possibilities: attack on the king or pressure on f6 (Qh4 possibly). Search for forced moves for black. It's a difficult position; you quickly lose count. Maybe the move Qh3 is also strong in connection with an indirect attack on the rook on c8. 1. Nxd5 and then 2. Qh3 is principally under consideration. First take on d5 in order to prevent black from making it easier for himself with Nxc3. The pawn on b2 is also still attacked. Playing for the win of a pawn is rather dangerous as the whole lot of white pawns also hangs; black will probably win back one of them easily. The capture on d4 is presumably not so dangerous (in the 1. Nxd5 and 2. Qf3 variation) for white; he can easily sacrifice that pawn and play Re1 with an attack. 1. Nxd5 and then maybe 2. Ng4? Also an idea. Calm move - then he takes on b2. Is that dangerous? It looks dismal for white to win back his pawn with advantage. Take on d5 and Rb1; or even 2. Rb1 immediately (sic). These variations do indeed appear to prevent Qxb2. It doesn't seem auspicious for black to take on b2. 1. Nc4 comes into consideration. Doesn't elicit much; the knight doesn't do much more there. 1. Nxd5 and 2. Rfe1 is also possible. (time pressure warning) Just go over the main points again. 1. Nxd5. [incorrect]
descriptions.De Groot, E4: First impression: white is somewhat better off 1. Nxc6 looks good in order to exchange the strong bishop, and next to exchange on d5, to get a favorable ending. Another possibility is to start a direct king's attack, possibly to be prepared by Qg3 and Ng4 or something like that. But most promising seems the former system. Let's calculate 1, Nxc6, 1... Rxc6, 2. Bxd5, 2... Nxd5,  3. Bxe7, 3... Nxe7; and then 4. Ne4 [-1.4] is an idea, in order to then plant a knight on f6 or on c5. Meanwhile does 2. Nxd5 or 2. Bxd5 produce any immediate advantage? Another method: 1. Nxc6 and 2. b4 - just to await what black will do. It is not so easy for black then. Something else. Nxd5 and exchange twice, then exchange on c8 and play Nxf7. No, that is also nothing special. 1. Bxd5, 1... Bxd5, 2. Nxd5 and 3. Bxf6 and 4. Nd7. Wins the exchange. I would play 1. Nxd5. If 1... Pxd5, then a flank attack or something like that. Probably best then is 2. Qf3. 1. Nxd5, 1... Bxd5; then 2. Bxd5 to win the exchange; so he is forced to take back with the pawn, and then I play 2. Qf3. Yes, 1. Nxd5. [incorrect]
descriptions.De Groot, E5: Let's see. What kind of opening has it been? Queen's gambit, with ...d5 and ...c5. Not sure. Black has a hole in his king's wing. So search for a good move. The isolated pawn is blockaded. And b2 is under attack. White must play on the attack. Look for a combination. 1. Bxf6, 1... Nxf6, 2. Nxg6, 2... fxg6, 3. Bxe6 and 4. queen takes pawn [??] perhaps? Or taking on d5 [??]? 1. Nxd5, then two, actually even three ways to retake. 1... Nxd5; then 2. Bxd5. Then he plays 2... Bxg5. How does that go on? Hold on: 3. f4, bishop away; 4. Bxc6, 4... bxc6, 5. Nd7 wins an exchange! White must aim for there: to weaken the d7 square; get rid of the bishop on c6 and the knight on f6. Just go over the 1. Nxd5 variation: yes, that's good! I play 1. Nxd5. [incorrect]
descriptions.De Groot, C2: The first thing that strikes me is the rook on the open c file; the queen on d3 - not unpleasant. This is not an easy position! Let me see. There's no threat, is there? The pawn on d4 is attacked but defended. The pawn on b2 is attacked. 1. Bh6 is possible, to chase away the rook. How solidly the pieces fit together! Everything is defended. Let's look at exchanges; what will remain then? 1. Nxd5, 2. Bxd5; then he takes back - with the pawn. Then play 3. Re1 [ambiguous] maybe? Then his knight is no longer defended (by his knight at d5), and then the bishop on e7 isn't defended so well. Should ...Bd8 have to be done, then the rooks are separated. It seems to be a system after all. 1. Nxd5, and if then 1... Nxd5 - then there's still nothing to it since his bishop on e7 is defended. 1. Nxd5, 1... Nxd5 - the situation is not inconvenient for black. Now let us tackle it from another angle. As the thing stands now, black cannot do much either. Oh, yes, he can take the pawn at b2. 1. h4 maybe. 1... Nh5; then 2. Bxe7, 2... Nxe7 may follow - that also comes to a dead end again. 3. g4 then? No, not best: the knight gets to f4. Calmly doubling the rooks is an idea too: 1. Rc2, then the pawn on b2 is defended as well. What can black do then? Maybe 1... Bd6 - then it has a somewhat better position. Then 2. Nxc6 and double the rooks. But black can do that too. Is there really no feasible plan for an attack? The bishop (on a2) stands on the diagonal - it reminds me of a game of my own where sacrifices on e6 were possible. Aren't there any possibilities for sacrifices on f6 or e6? But then it would first be necessary to get the knight on d5 out of the way. That does succeed, e.g.: 1. Nxd5, 1... Nxd5, 2. Bxe7, 2... Nxe7, 3. Nxg6? No, for now his knight on e7 once again defends his g6. Let's start over with : 1. Bh6. Another little plan: 1... rook goes; 2. Ne4, 2... Nxe4, 3. Qxe4 - what have you then? 1. h4 may be in order to still play to break open the king's side. 1... Nh5, then exchange on d5. Yes, but this must then be preceded by 1. Bh6 probably. Wait a moment, if Nxd5, then ...Bb5 - unappetizing. Have a look: 1. Bh6, rook moves, 2. Nxd5, 2... Bb5 - doesn't work now because of taking on e7 with check and then Nxg6+, and again Nxg6+ and Qxh6+ (sic); we just let him have the rook on f8. Yes, I play 1. Bh6. [incorrect]
descriptions.De Groot, C5: (blind recount after 15 seconds of looking at the position. After that the normal thinking aloud procedure) Began with a maze of pieces. After tat: white has an attacking position - concentration of queen, bishop(s), and the knight on e5 on the king's position, weakened through ...g6. Then looked if there were also immediate chestnuts by black to fear; didn't see any, idea that there aren't any there. Then: now I'll have to start thinking of a combination, but I'm afraid that there are no immediate winning possibilities. The stand: I have that in my head more in lines than on squares. Black: castled position, pawn on g6. Black bishop bangs his head against the pawn on e6; black queen and rook on the queen's wing. White: castled position, queen and bishop on long diagonal, queen on d3, bishop on a2, other bishop on the a1-h8 diagonal. Wait a minute, there is no place for it: the knight's on c3, pawn on d4, knight's on e5; no, it wasn't there. Where then? On g5? Yes, it must have been there. Concerning moves I looked briefly at 1. Bh6, followed by a knight move, sacrifice on f7 or g7 and then a queen move. (On being shown the position he was struck by: the bishop on c6 was otherwise; thought the b file was open; the knight on d5 was solidly defended!) Thinking aloud: First the combinatorial stuff there with 1. Bh6; doesn't appear so very favorable, still too well fortified. (rather long pause) Had 1. Qf3 in mind. No, that doesn't work, then he takes on d4. No, that whole setup's a bit too fragile for that. Now to try and open up the king's side a bit more: exchange on d5 (1. Nxd5); what then? 1... Nxd5 and then you must exchange the bishop on e7; then too much goes off and it doesn't help much. Maybe 1. Bh6 after all to chase away the rook on f8 (protecting f7). 1. Bh6, 1... Rfe8 - then is 2. Nxg6 not sufficient. Otherwise 1. Bh6 wasn't really so crazy, because if I exchange on d5, then 1... Nxd5 and the bishop exchange, not so agreeable. 1. Bh6 in order to shun that and then afterwards take on d5? I'm now looking at 1. Ne4, 1... Nxe4; no, because that doesn't help things. Exchanging is the simplest. Not good. The whole thing is a matter of maintaining the pressure. 1. Nxd5, 1... Nxd5, 2. Bxe7, 2... Nxe7. What to do then? Holy on, now we're coming to still quite another idea: 1. Qh3, to start with a kind of pin of the pawn on e6 - after pawn takes on d5 then the diagonal to c8 opens up. 1. Qh3 to be followed by taking on d5; then after pawn retakes on d5, the diagonal's open. Oh, no, 1. Qh3 doesn't go because of the pawn on d4. Bah, the thing doesn't become any better from that. (E: what are you thinking about) Now about the queen pawn again. I saw in the beginning already that b2 is attacked, but that didn't seem important to me; that's why didn't give it a further thought. We cannot let him take the d pawn.  (on being asked:) Still no convergence to one or another particular move. I have the awkward feeling that if I want to start something I immediately get simplifications and then my attack is gone. So maybe I should think about a positional move, but when I make a positional move, then black can himself simplify. If I must play safely 1. b4 or some such thing; if on the attack then 1. h4, for example. What would the follow-up of 1. h4 be? No, it doesn't suit me; gives too many counterchances. Takes too long. Let's contemplate building up the attack with 1. Bb1 - but then the queen's in front, that's wrong; that's overdoing it a bit for sacrificial combinations on g6. If the attack shall be, then it must be somewhat more circumspect. 1. Ne2 maybe, to g3, pawn h4, and afterwards h5 - doesn't work, then the queen gets in on b2. If I want to keep hold of that attack, then 1. Bh6 really does come into consideration, in order to keep hold of the pawns and the pressure. And then, for instance, make a safe move b4 and possibly Ne2. 1. Bh6 and 2. b4 probably. (on being asked:) In a game I would still keep looking, but it would presumably come to that. (long pause) Let's see. (time pressure remark) First 1. a4 maybe, in order to prevent his bishop from coming to b5. If I chop off that bishop some time, what then? Wait a minute, I can make him choose. I must get rid of that bishop on c6: too many menacing possibilities. 1. Nxc6 as a first move to see how he'd take back. 1... Qxc6, then b4's superfluous. And on 1... Rxc6 or 1... bxc6, then he has lost the bishop at any rate, then at least my knight on c3 can get into stride. Well, that's not such a completely crazy idea at all. Black can't start so much. (pause) What remains after total simplification? Don't believe that that's favorable, then I don't stand soundly. 1. Nxc6; possibly Re1 [ambiguous] after it if holes turn up on the e file. Yes, 1. Nxc6. [incorrect]
